overview.title: Reject bad work before changing the queue

nodes.label: Check the final state
code: // 101 is invalid; 8 is rejected as full.

overview.explanation: Solid arrows show conditional execution and the final check. Each submit call returns before the next call begins; this example has no concurrent producer.

focus.title: Check first, mutate second
focus.code:
std::vector<int> jobs{4};constexpr std::size_t capacity=2;
    auto submit=[&](int x){if(x<0||x>100||jobs.size()==capacity)return false;jobs.push_back(x);return true;};
explain: The queue starts with 4. constexpr makes capacity a compile-time constant equal to two.
[&] borrows jobs and capacity. || means logical OR; if any guard is true, return false ends the call. Only a passing call reaches push_back and returns true.
focus.what: Admission is a boundary: reject inputs outside 0–100 and requests that would exceed capacity.
focus.where: The lambda runs three times from the next source line.
focus.why: Keeping checks before mutation makes rejection easy to reason about and test.
focus.invariant: At this boundary, jobs.size() never exceeds two and a rejected call preserves its previous state.
focus.risk: Pushing first and checking later would briefly or permanently violate capacity. Concurrent callers would need synchronization; this code is a single-thread model.

focus.title: Test results and state together
explain: The calls run in order: 7 is accepted, 101 is invalid, and 8 finds the queue full.
The explicit comparison returns failure status 1 unless the vector is exactly {4,7}.
boolalpha prints true/false. The observed results are accepted=true, invalid=false, full=false, count=2.
focus.what: The test checks both returned decisions and the state those decisions leave behind.
focus.where: The fixture is inside main, after all three submissions.
focus.why: A boolean alone could hide an unwanted state change; checking the vector catches it.
focus.invariant: Only one additional job is stored. Invalid and full calls leave it unchanged.
focus.risk: Calling false an error category loses the distinction between invalid input and temporary saturation; Book VIII’s outcome type addresses that need.
